credit: Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team / NASA GSFC · public domain · resized
alt: Hawaiian islands with greener windward slopes, drier leeward slopes and silvery sunglint on the Pacific.
caption: Terra MODIS, 27 May 2003. Northeasterly trade winds favour wetter, greener windward slopes; leeward slopes are drier. The bright ocean is sunglint.

credit: Karthoo / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: The Wutach flows through a narrow, wooded gorge below exposed rock walls in the Black Forest.
caption: Wutach Gorge, Germany. Capture diverted drainage from the Danube system towards the Rhine; subsequent incision cut this gorge.

credit: none (Landsat) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: False-colour Landsat image of the Lena Delta with many branching distributaries and islands.
caption: Landsat's view of the Lena Delta, 2000. Distributaries spread sediment into the Arctic Ocean. The image combines infrared and red bands.

credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Rounded potholes cut into dark bedrock beside flowing water in the Presque Isle River, Michigan.
caption: Presque Isle River, Michigan. Swirling, sediment-laden water has drilled potholes into the bedrock of this river in the Upper Peninsula, near Lake Superior.

credit: Walter Siegmund / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
alt: Floodwater from the Stillaguamish River surrounds a picnic table and trees.
caption: The South Fork Stillaguamish River in flood. Water spreads beyond the usual channel when discharge exceeds channel capacity.

credit: NASA/Kjell Lindgren / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: The muddy Ucayali River winds through forest in Peru, with abandoned bends beside the active channel.
caption: Ucayali River, Peru, photographed from the ISS. Meander migration leaves cut-offs and abandoned channels across the floodplain.

credit: Kevin M. Gill / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: A rounded specimen of augen gneiss with pale mineral eyes enclosed in dark, folded bands.
caption: Augen gneiss: deformation and metamorphism organise minerals into bands around larger crystals. Rock-cycle pathways need not follow one fixed loop.

credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: South African city lights beneath a curved glowing atmospheric horizon and stars, viewed from the ISS.
caption: South Africa at night, seen from the ISS. Earth's rotation carries every place through daylight and darkness each day.

credit: National Oceanic & Atmospheric Adminstration (NOAA) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Rounded pillow lava on a fissured seafloor at the Galápagos Rift, photographed by a NOAA expedition.
caption: NOAA, Galápagos Rift, 21 July 2011. Lava quenched in seawater forms pillows close to a spreading centre, where new oceanic crust is built.

credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
caption: Meteosat-9 SEVIRI, 21 December 2010. The tilted day–night boundary shows the Southern Hemisphere having longer days. Axial tilt, not a change in Earth–Sun distance, causes this seasonal pattern.

credit: Jan Nyssen, Sander Tielens, Tesfamichael Gebreyohannes, Tigist Araya, Kassa Teka, Johan Van de Wauw, Karen Degeyndt, Katrien Descheemaeker, Kassa Amare, Mitiku Haile, Amanuel Zenebe, Neil Munro, Kristine Walraevens, Kindeya Gebrehiwot, Jean Poesen, Amaury Frankl, Alemtsehay Tsegay, Jozef Deckers / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
alt: Field photographs of red and black soils at different positions on the Addi Selam hillslope in Ethiopia.
caption: Addi Selam, Ethiopia (published field figure). A: red soil on the upper slope near the town; B: dark, clay-rich soil on the gentler lower ground. Slope position changes drainage and how material moves, so the soils differ along the catena.

credit: Willem van Aken, CSIRO / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0 · resized
alt: Bare eroded soil with small gullies on a hillslope near Charters Towers, Queensland.
caption: Hillslope gully and sheet erosion near Charters Towers, Queensland, documented by CSIRO. Loss of cover exposes soil to runoff.

credit: Leonhard Lenz / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
alt: An exposed soil profile beneath woodland at Wuhlheide in Berlin, with a measuring tape against the face.
caption: A measured field profile in Wuhlheide, Berlin. Colour and texture vary down the soil; horizon boundaries must be identified from field evidence.

credit: NPS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: National Park Service soil scientists examine a freshly sampled soil profile and record its texture.
caption: NPS fieldwork at Chesapeake and Ohio Canal National Historical Park. Texture describes the proportions of sand, silt and clay in the mineral soil.

credit: Photograph by Clem Rutter, Rochester, Kent. (www.clemrutter.net). / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: A spherical sundial with hour markings and a movable gnomon at Green's Windmill, Nottingham.
caption: A working sundial at Green's Windmill, Nottingham. A gnomon's shadow connects the Sun's apparent direction with local solar time.

credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Saturn and its broad rings in a natural-colour mosaic photographed by the Cassini spacecraft.
caption: Cassini, 6 October 2004: a natural-colour mosaic of Saturn and its rings. The rings are a thin disc of orbiting particles.

credit: NOAA Photo Library / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: An aerial view of damaged buildings and washed-over land on the Bolivar Peninsula after Hurricane Ike.
caption: Bolivar Peninsula, Texas, September 2008. NOAA documented coastal damage from Hurricane Ike's storm surge.

credit: NASA/SDO, ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: Extreme-ultraviolet observation of the full Sun showing bright active regions, displayed in yellow.
caption: SDO's Atmospheric Imaging Assembly, 18 December 2015. This false-colour ultraviolet observation reveals the hot solar atmosphere, not the Sun's visible colour.

credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · Aqua MODIS / EOSDIS · public domain · resized
alt: Afternoon cumulus clouds over Sri Lanka, observed by Aqua MODIS on 9 April 2013.
caption: Aqua MODIS, 9 April 2013. Cumulus clouds form over Sri Lanka while the surrounding sea stays clear. Daytime heating of the land drives a sea breeze inland, where the air rises.

credit: owamux / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Circular plates of new pancake ice cover the surface of the western Ross Sea in Antarctica.
caption: New sea ice forming in the Ross Sea. Freezing rejects much of the salt into the surrounding water, increasing its density and helping drive polar overturning.

credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: GOES-East satellite view of the Americas with tropical cloud bands and midlatitude weather systems.
caption: GOES-East cloud data for 22 April 2014, laid over a cloud-free satellite image of land and ocean, so the whole disc is shown lit. Cloud belts reveal aspects of the global circulation; a single image does not outline every atmospheric cell.

credit: Dennis G. Jarvis / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: A fishing boat rests on exposed mud beside a wharf at low tide in Nova Scotia.
caption: Low tide at Waterford on St Mary's Bay, Nova Scotia. The exposed harbour floor makes tidal range visible.

credit: NASA astronaut Ed Lu / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: The clear eye and tall spiral cloud walls of Hurricane Isabel, photographed from the ISS.
caption: Astronaut Ed Lu photographed Hurricane Isabel on 13 September 2003. The eye is surrounded by the eyewall's deep convective clouds.

credit: Mass Communication Specialist 3rd Class Dylan McCord / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Aerial view of debris, damaged buildings and flooded land at a fishing port in Kesennuma after the 2011 tsunami.
caption: Kesennuma, Japan, after the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami. The photograph shows the damage left by inundation, not the tsunami wave itself.

credit: NASA, ESA, J. Dalcanton, B.F. Williams, and L.C. Johnson (University of Washington), the PHAT team, and R. Gendler / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: A Hubble mosaic of Andromeda's bright central region, dark dust lanes and densely packed stars.
caption: NASA/ESA Hubble mosaic of the Andromeda Galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away. Individual stars and dust lanes are visible.

credit: Jim D. Griggs, HVO (USGS) staff photographer[1][2] / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: An arching orange lava fountain erupts from a vent on Kīlauea amid dark cooling lava.
caption: A lava fountain about 10 metres high at Kīlauea, photographed by USGS on 25 February 1983. Magma reaches the surface here, but the mantle beneath is almost entirely solid.

credit: Bernard Spragg. NZ from Christchurch, New Zealand / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Wisps of low fog rise above a calm lake on a frosty morning, with trees reflected in the water.
caption: Evaporation fog over a lake. Water evaporating from the warmer lake condenses into tiny droplets in the cold air above; the fog is droplets, not invisible water vapour.

credit: Dexter Perkins / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
alt: Rounded remnants of granite emerge from loose weathered material in an exposed rock profile.
caption: Weathered granite. As its minerals break down, solid rock gradually turns into loose weathered material.

credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Long fault-bounded valleys and escarpments in Kenya's East African Rift, viewed from the ISS.
caption: The East African Rift in Kenya: continental extension is an opening stage of a possible ocean-basin cycle. A rift does not inevitably become an ocean.

credit: Geographer / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: An orange windsock extends above a field beside the path to Green Lane Farm.
caption: A windsock responds to moving air. Its open mouth faces into the wind; meteorological wind direction names where the air comes from.

credit: NASA Astronaut photograph from ISS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Crescent-shaped dunes around Lagoa dos Barros on Brazil's Atlantic coast, seen from the ISS.
caption: Wind shapes barchan dunes beside Lagoa dos Barros, Brazil. The crescent tips point downwind.

credit: Arthur Rothstein / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A car on a Texas Panhandle road beneath a wall of airborne dust during the Dust Bowl.
caption: Texas Panhandle during the 1930s Dust Bowl. Wind lifted fine topsoil from dry, bare fields: deflation removed the soil and carried the dust away in suspension.

credit: Rosa Cabecinhas and Alcino Cunha / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: A sharp dune crest and rippled sand at Erg Chebbi, Morocco.
caption: Erg Chebbi, Morocco: a sand sea where wind-blown sand has built up into large dunes. Most of the Sahara is rock or gravel rather than erg.

credit: Chris M Morris / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: A mesquite shrub grows on a mound of trapped sand in the Mojave Desert.
caption: Mesquite in Mojave National Preserve, California. Vegetation traps wind-blown sand and can build a small dune called a nabkha.

credit: matteo caprari / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Wind-blown sand and ripples in Libya's desert.
caption: Wind-blown sand streams across rippled dunes in Libya. Most moving grains travel in short hops just above the surface; this hopping is saltation.

credit: Arthur Rothstein / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A car on a Texas Panhandle road beneath a wall of airborne dust during the Dust Bowl.
caption: A Dust Bowl dust storm in the Texas Panhandle. Turbulent wind keeps the finest particles aloft in suspension, so they can travel far beyond their source fields.

credit: lwtt93 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Long, wind-eroded rock ridges rise above the desert at Dunhuang, China.
caption: Yardangs at Dunhuang, China. Persistent wind erosion shapes elongated ridges in relatively soft rock or sediment.

credit: Paul Wynter / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Graw DFM radiosondes and a radio receiver arranged on a table.
caption: Balloon-borne radiosondes transmit measurements of the atmosphere. Profiles of temperature, humidity and pressure help locate inversions and estimate lapse rates.

credit: NASA / Expedition 66 crew · ISS066-E-86970 · public domain · resized
alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
caption: Earth's thin atmosphere seen edge-on from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Scattered sunlight lights the lower layers; the coloured bands do not mark exact layer boundaries.

credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio - Amy Moran, Lauren Dauphin, Paul Newman, Katie Jepson, Aaron E. Lepsch / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: NASA map of low ozone concentrations over Antarctica in September 2023.
caption: NASA Ozone Watch and GEOS-5, 21 September 2023. The ozone hole is a region of depleted stratospheric ozone; the colours show ozone amounts, not a visible gap.

credit: Paul Wynter / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Graw DFM radiosondes and a radio receiver arranged on a table.
caption: Balloon-borne radiosondes transmit measurements of the atmosphere. Profiles of temperature, humidity and pressure help locate inversions and estimate lapse rates.

alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
caption: Earth's thin atmosphere seen edge-on from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Scattered sunlight lights the lower layers; the coloured bands do not mark exact layer boundaries.

credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A green auroral band glows below the International Space Station above the southern Indian Ocean.
caption: An ISS photograph of aurora north of Antarctica. Energetic particles excite upper-atmosphere gases; the green light is emitted by the atmosphere, not reflected sunlight.

credit: NASA / Expedition 66 crew · ISS066-E-86970 · public domain · resized
alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
caption: Earth's thin atmosphere seen edge-on from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Scattered sunlight lights the lower layers; the coloured bands do not mark exact layer boundaries.

credit: NASA / Expedition 66 crew · ISS066-E-86970 · public domain · resized
alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
caption: Earth's thin atmosphere seen edge-on from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Scattered sunlight lights the lower layers; the coloured bands do not mark exact layer boundaries.

credit: Poyt448 Peter Woodard / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Fallen leaves and organic litter beneath white beech trees in New South Wales, Australia.
caption: White beech leaf litter at Carowiry Creek, New South Wales. Organic material on the forest floor stores carbon and provides material for decomposition.

credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Scientific Visualization Studio · public domain · resized
alt: NASA CERES map of reflected shortwave radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a 0–385 W m⁻² colour scale.
caption: NASA CERES observations, 2000–2015 mean. Colours show sunlight reflected by the Earth system in W m⁻². This is outgoing shortwave flux, not incoming solar irradiance or albedo itself.

credit: Edal Anton Lefterov / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Brown coal exposed at Chukurovo in Bulgaria.
caption: Lignite at Chukurovo, Bulgaria. This fossil fuel formed from buried plant material; combustion transfers its stored carbon to the atmosphere.

credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
caption: Forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon. Leaves intercept falling rain and absorb sunlight for photosynthesis, storing carbon in living plants.

credit: Poyt448 Peter Woodard / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Fallen leaves and organic litter beneath white beech trees in New South Wales, Australia.
caption: White beech leaf litter at Carowiry Creek, New South Wales. Organic material on the forest floor stores carbon and provides material for decomposition.

credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
caption: Layered rocks in the Grand Canyon record deep time and the slow carbon cycle. Lithification turns sediment into rock, and the inner gorge exposes much older Precambrian basement.

credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
caption: Tropical forest at Bodiman, Cameroon: living vegetation is a carbon store, exchanging carbon with the air and soil.

credit: Dexter Perkins / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
alt: Rounded remnants of granite emerge from loose weathered material in an exposed rock profile.
caption: Weathered granite. As its minerals break down, solid rock gradually turns into loose weathered material.

credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
caption: Tropical forest at Bodiman, Cameroon, an example of rainforest vegetation. An Af climate is defined by long-term monthly temperature and rainfall, not by vegetation alone.

credit: Bjørn Christian Tørrissen / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Grassland with scattered acacia trees in Serengeti National Park, Tanzania.
caption: Serengeti savanna: seasonal rainfall helps explain the balance between grasses and scattered trees.

credit: Luca Galuzzi (Lucag) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
alt: Tall orange sand dunes under a clear sky at Sossusvlei, Namibia.
caption: Sossusvlei dunes, Namib Desert. Wind moves sand grains by saltation (bouncing) and surface creep, building dunes over time.

credit: Manfred Heyde / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Green fields and wooded valleys on Exmoor in North Devon.
caption: Exmoor, North Devon: a landscape within the Cfb oceanic climate region. Köppen classes use long-term monthly temperature and precipitation, not the weather on the day of the photograph.

credit: James T M Towill / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Weather instruments inside the enclosure at Charterhall in the Scottish Borders.
caption: Charterhall weather station, Scotland. Standardised instruments measure local conditions; climate describes their statistics over many years.

credit: Richard Mortel / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Open grassland and sparsely vegetated hills near Jargalant, northern Mongolia.
caption: Steppe near Jargalant, Mongolia, far from the moderating influence of the sea. Continental interiors usually have a large annual temperature range.

credit: Manfred Heyde / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Green fields and wooded valleys on Exmoor in North Devon.
caption: Exmoor, North Devon: a landscape within the Cfb oceanic climate region. Köppen classes use long-term monthly temperature and precipitation, not the weather on the day of the photograph.

credit: Alvesgaspar / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
alt: A breaking wave curls and foams along the coast at Porto Covo, Portugal.
caption: A breaking wave at Porto Covo, Portugal. Whether waves build up or erode a beach depends on the balance of swash and backwash over many waves, which one photograph cannot show.

credit: Alvesgaspar / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
alt: A breaking wave curls and foams along the coast at Porto Covo, Portugal.
caption: A breaking wave at Porto Covo, Portugal. In shallow water a wave slows and steepens; its crest eventually breaks.

credit: Iraphne R. Childs / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: A groyne extends across the beach at Tallebudgera Creek on Australia's Gold Coast.
caption: Tallebudgera Creek, Gold Coast, in the 1980s. A groyne interrupts sediment movement along a beach and can change sediment supply farther down-drift.

credit: Chris / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Aerial photograph of Spurn Point curving across the Humber estuary entrance.
caption: Spurn Point, England, photographed in 2024. Longshore drift feeds this spit across the mouth of the Humber estuary.

credit: Chris / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Aerial photograph of Spurn Point curving across the Humber estuary entrance.
caption: Spurn Point, England, photographed in 2024. Longshore drift feeds this spit across the mouth of the Humber estuary.

credit: Chris / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Aerial photograph of Spurn Point curving across the Humber estuary entrance.
caption: Spurn Point, England, photographed in 2024. Longshore drift feeds this spit across the mouth of the Humber estuary.

credit: Jakub Hałun / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: The isolated rock stack Hvítserkur rises from shallow coastal water in northwestern Iceland.
caption: Hvítserkur, Iceland: a sea stack with openings eroded through its base.

credit: Lewis Clarke / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: White chalk cliffs, offshore remnants and a wave-cut base near the Pinnacles in Purbeck.
caption: The Pinnacles coast, Purbeck, Dorset. Erosion leaves isolated stacks and lower remnants called stumps beside the retreating chalk cliffs.

credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: crust shortened and thickened as India collided with Eurasia.

credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: NOAA bathymetry map of the South Atlantic showing continental shelves and the mid-ocean ridge.
caption: NOAA South Atlantic bathymetry. Colour represents seafloor depth, revealing continental margins, abyssal basins and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
caption: Mantle peridotite carried to the surface as a xenolith in volcanic rock: a sample of solid upper mantle, not crust. The lithosphere includes the crust and the rigid uppermost mantle.

credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: A dark Glossopteris fossil leaf from Permian rocks in Antarctica, with a branching vein network.
caption: Permian Glossopteris leaf from Antarctica. Related fossils on separated southern continents are evidence that these lands were once joined within Gondwana, which formed part of Pangaea.

credit: National Oceanic & Atmospheric Adminstration (NOAA) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized

caption: NOAA, Galápagos Rift, 21 July 2011. Lava quenched in seawater forms pillows close to a spreading centre, where new oceanic crust is built.

caption: Part of a USGS topographic map near Yosemite Creek, California. Benchmarks (BM) and crosses give spot heights in feet, labelled contours such as 7400 and 7600 show the interval, and contours bend around spurs and valleys.

caption: ASTER false-colour image, 24 September 2005: tributaries cut into sandstone in Canyonlands, Utah. Plants along the valley floors show up red. The branching network carries water towards the Colorado River (top left).

caption: The historic Greenwich Meridian marker. Longitude is measured from here, and every 15° of longitude is about one hour of solar time.

alt: Big and Little Diomede islands in the Bering Strait, between snow-covered Russia and Alaska, seen by Landsat 8.
caption: Landsat image of the Diomede Islands, either side of the International Date Line: a convention where the calendar date changes, not a physical line.

credit: Lapos71 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: First-quarter Moon photographed from Calabria, with the right half of the visible lunar disc sunlit.
caption: A first-quarter Moon: half the visible disc is lit when the Moon is about 90° from the Sun in our sky, as in the model's quarter position.

credit: Luc Viatour / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Nearly full Moon photographed from Hamois, Belgium, with dark maria and bright cratered highlands.
caption: A nearly full Moon, lit almost completely because it lies roughly opposite the Sun. Earth's shadow does not cause the phase.

alt: Aerial view of abandoned buildings at the Kola Superdeep Borehole site in Russia in 2020.
caption: The Kola Superdeep Borehole site. At 12.262 km it is the deepest hole ever drilled, yet it did not get through the continental crust.

alt: Swarm-derived maps compare Earth's magnetic field intensity in 2014 and 2025, with a scale in nanotesla.
caption: Maps of magnetic-field strength at Earth's surface in 2014 and 2025, modelled from Swarm satellite measurements (colours show nanotesla). The field is generated mainly by moving liquid iron in the outer core, not by a permanent bar magnet.

credit: Thomas Pratt, USGS. Public domain. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: USGS scientists install a field seismometer at Sabana Yeguas, Puerto Rico.
caption: A seismometer being installed in Puerto Rico. Recorded P- and S-wave arrivals are the main evidence for the layers in the model.

alt: Aerial view of the San Andreas Fault cutting across dry hills in California.
caption: The San Andreas Fault, California: a transform boundary where the plates slide past each other horizontally.

credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: a convergent boundary where continental crust has been shortened and thickened in a collision.

alt: NOAA seafloor relief map around Puerto Rico identifies the deep Puerto Rico Trench and nearby plate boundary.
caption: NOAA seafloor relief of the Puerto Rico Trench, where the North American Plate meets the Caribbean Plate at an oblique convergent boundary. Colours show measured depth with vertical relief exaggerated; the labels and boundary lines are added interpretation.

credit: Donnchadh H / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: Rounded hills and fields around the Vale of Edale, viewed from Grindslow Knoll.
caption: The Vale of Edale and Lose Hill, Peak District. Compare the real valley and spur shapes with the contour patterns the model draws.

alt: USGS topographic map extract showing Yosemite Creek, a campground, contours and coordinate markings.
caption: A USGS topographic sheet of Yosemite Creek. Tightly packed contours mark steep valley sides; widely spaced ones mark gentle ground.

credit: Brian Deegan / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Water falls through a narrow rocky step into a dark plunge pool at Cwmorthin, Wales.
caption: A waterfall and plunge pool at Cwmorthin, Wales: a steep step typical of an upper course, where the long profile is steepest.

credit: Jocelyn Augustino / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A raised embankment separates floodwater from farmland beside the Mississippi at Hannibal, Missouri.
caption: The Mississippi at Hannibal, Missouri: a wide lowland river on a gentle gradient, bordered by an engineered levee.

credit: none (Landsat) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: False-colour Landsat image of the Lena Delta with many branching distributaries and islands.
caption: False-colour Landsat image of the Lena Delta, Russia, where the river reaches base level and deposits its load.

credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
caption: Forest canopy in Cameroon. Leaves intercept rainfall and return water to the air by transpiration.

credit: USFS employees / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped and resized
alt: Melting snow patches and a stream near Fourth of July Lake in Idaho's Sawtooth Mountains.
caption: Snowmelt feeding a stream in Idaho: water released from a snow store into surface flow.

credit: Aravind Sivaraj / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: A hand pump used to draw groundwater at Perambalur, India.
caption: A groundwater hand pump in India. Abstraction removes water from the groundwater store.

credit: NASA/JHUAPL / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: MESSENGER global mosaic of Mercury showing its cratered surface.
caption: NASA MESSENGER mosaic of Mercury, a small rocky terrestrial planet close to the Sun.

credit: NASA/JPL / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Voyager 2 image of Neptune's blue disc showing cloud bands and the Great Dark Spot.
caption: Voyager 2 image of Neptune, an ice giant about 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth. Its displayed colour has been processed.

credit: NASA/Apollo 17 crew; taken by either Harrison Schmitt or Ron Evans / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: The fully sunlit Earth showing Africa, Arabia, Antarctica and swirling clouds in the Apollo 17 photograph.
caption: Earth photographed by Apollo 17: the largest of the four rocky terrestrial planets.

credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: An SDO observation of the solar photosphere showing a large dark sunspot group.
caption: NASA SDO view of the photosphere with a large sunspot group: the visible surface that supplies the sunlight in the model.

alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
caption: Meteosat satellite image at the December solstice. Sunlight strikes the southern hemisphere more directly, so equal beams spread over smaller areas there.

credit: Zdeněk Bardon/ESO / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: A long-exposure photograph of Orion's stars, red emission nebulae and dark dust clouds.
caption: Stars and nebulae in Orion. Stars that look close together in the sky can lie hundreds of light-years apart.

alt: A sequence of dark Venus silhouettes crosses the Sun in SDO ultraviolet observations.
caption: SDO image sequence of Venus crossing the Sun in 2012. Timing such transits helped astronomers measure the astronomical unit.

credit: Wilson44691 / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Fossilised Ogyopsis klotzi trilobite preserved in dark shale.
caption: A Middle Cambrian trilobite, roughly 500 million years old, from the Mount Stephen beds, Canada. Fossils mark positions on the timeline.

alt: Close-up of a rock face in the Scollard Formation, Alberta, with a thin pale clay layer just below a black coal seam.
caption: The K–Pg boundary in Alberta, about 66 million years ago, when the non-bird dinosaurs disappeared.

credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
caption: The Grand Canyon exposes a long stack of rock layers, but unconformities mean parts of the record are missing.

alt: The Moon appears copper-red during a lunar eclipse viewed from Merritt Island, Florida.
caption: A total lunar eclipse in January 2000. The Moon lies in Earth's umbra and is lit only by reddened light refracted through Earth's atmosphere.

alt: A sequence of dark Venus silhouettes crosses the Sun in SDO ultraviolet observations.
caption: Venus crossing the Sun in 2012. Like an eclipse, a transit needs the bodies to line up near an orbital node.

alt: First-quarter Moon photographed from Calabria, with the right half of the visible lunar disc sunlit.
caption: A first-quarter Moon. With the Sun and Moon at right angles, their tidal effects partly cancel, favouring neap tides.

credit: Luc Viatour / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Nearly full Moon photographed from Hamois, Belgium, with dark maria and bright cratered highlands.
caption: A nearly full Moon. Near full and new Moon the Sun and Moon line up, favouring spring tides with a larger range.

alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
caption: Meteosat satellite image at the December solstice. The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn, so northern noon altitudes are at their lowest.

alt: Meteosat view of Earth's nearly north–south day–night boundary at the March equinox.
caption: Meteosat satellite image at the March equinox. The Sun is overhead at the equator, and the noon altitude at any latitude is 90° minus the latitude.

alt: A dark Glossopteris fossil leaf from Permian rocks in Antarctica, with a branching vein network.
caption: A Glossopteris leaf fossil from Antarctica. The same plant fossils on separate southern continents suggest they were once joined in Pangaea.

alt: NOAA bathymetry map of the South Atlantic showing continental shelves and the mid-ocean ridge.

alt: Steam and orange microbial mats around Grand Prismatic Spring in Yellowstone National Park.
caption: Grand Prismatic Spring, Yellowstone: hydrothermal activity above a continental hotspot, inside the North American Plate.

caption: NOAA multibeam survey of an Arctic seamount, shown in 3D with colours for depth; the vertical scale is probably exaggerated. Volcanoes carried away from a hotspot can cool and sink to become seamounts, although not every seamount forms this way.

alt: NOAA bathymetry map of the South Atlantic showing continental shelves and the mid-ocean ridge.
caption: NOAA bathymetry of the South Atlantic, showing the Mid-Atlantic Ridge running midway between the continents.

alt: Steep dark rock walls border the Almannagjá rift at Þingvellir, Iceland.

alt: A hand pump used to draw groundwater at Perambalur, India.
caption: A hand pump in India. Pumping abstracts groundwater and can create a cone of depression around the well.

alt: The Aletsch Glacier curves through a steep Alpine valley, with dark medial moraines running along its surface.
caption: The Aletsch Glacier, Switzerland. Ice sheets far thicker than this pressed the crust down, and it rebounds when the ice melts.

alt: Satellite image of the parallel folded ridges of the Appalachian Mountains and Chesapeake Bay.

alt: NOAA bathymetry map of the South Atlantic showing continental shelves and the mid-ocean ridge.
caption: NOAA bathymetry of the South Atlantic: passive margins on both sides of an ocean that opened as Africa and South America rifted apart.

alt: Dry, deeply dissected loess slopes near Hunyuan in Shanxi, China.
caption: Loess hills in Shanxi, China, for comparison: here running water, not wind, has cut deep gullies into wind-deposited silt.

credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: ASTER satellite image of branching tributary valleys near the Colorado River in Canyonlands, Utah.
caption: ASTER satellite image of tributaries draining to the Colorado River in Canyonlands, Utah, upstream of Lake Powell.

credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
caption: The Grand Canyon, Arizona, between Lake Powell and Lake Mead. Water released from Glen Canyon Dam flows through it on its way to Lake Mead.

credit: Strebe / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite imagery displayed in a Mollweide projection with a graticule.
caption: A world map with its graticule. The central meridian of this Mollweide map is the prime meridian through Greenwich, from which longitude is measured east and west.

credit: Photograph by Clem Rutter, Rochester, Kent. (www.clemrutter.net). / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: A spherical sundial with hour markings and a movable gnomon at Green's Windmill, Nottingham.
caption: A sundial at Green's Windmill, Nottingham, about 1.2° west of Greenwich. It shows local solar time, which here runs about four and a half minutes behind solar time at Greenwich.

credit: Joshua Stevens / NASA Earth Observatory, Landsat data: USGS · public domain · resized
alt: Big and Little Diomede islands in the Bering Strait, between snow-covered Russia and Alaska, seen by Landsat 8.
caption: Landsat 8 image of the Diomede Islands in the Bering Strait. Little Diomede (US) and Big Diomede (Russia) lie either side of the International Date Line, under 4 km apart but nearly a day apart on the clock.

credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
alt: Meteosat view of Earth's nearly north–south day–night boundary at the March equinox.
caption: Meteosat-9 satellite image at the March equinox. It illustrates the process, not the USA: as Earth rotates eastward, the day–night boundary sweeps westward across places at different longitudes.

credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
caption: A mantle xenolith from Peridot Mesa, Arizona, not Kola. Rock from the mantle reaches the surface only when magma carries it up; drilling has never reached the mantle.

credit: Thomas Pratt, USGS. Public domain. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: USGS scientists install a field seismometer at Sabana Yeguas, Puerto Rico.
caption: A USGS seismometer being installed in Puerto Rico. Seismic waves recorded by instruments like this reveal layers far deeper than the Kola borehole's 12 km.

credit: Petersrockypics / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Snow on Gallt y Wenallt above mist in Nant Gwynant, Eryri / Snowdonia.
caption: Nant Gwynant in Eryri. Steep valley sides like these raise the local horizon, so the Moon appears later than it would over flat ground.

credit: Lapos71 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: First-quarter Moon photographed from Calabria, with the right half of the visible lunar disc sunlit.
caption: First-quarter Moon photographed from Calabria, Italy. The phase depends on Sun–Earth–Moon geometry, so observers in Eryri see the same half-lit disc at the same time.

credit: Diliff / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Yosemite Valley's forested floor between steep granite walls, viewed from Tunnel View.
caption: Yosemite Valley from Tunnel View. The high granite walls hide the horizon, delaying when a rising full Moon becomes visible from the valley floor.

credit: NASA Kennedy Space Center, KSC-00PP-0096 · public domain · via Wikimedia Commons · resized
alt: The Moon appears copper-red during a lunar eclipse viewed from Merritt Island, Florida.
caption: Lunar eclipse of 20 January 2000, photographed from Florida. An eclipse happens only when a full Moon lies near a node of its inclined orbit; most full Moons miss Earth's shadow.

credit: Jesse Allen / NASA Earth Observatory · Landsat · public domain · resized
alt: Landsat view of the northern Gulf of Mexico coast, with barrier islands off Mississippi and Alabama and the faint Chandeleur arc off Louisiana.
caption: Landsat image of the northern Gulf coast (colours enhanced). Like the Outer Banks, the narrow barrier islands off Mississippi and Alabama (top) and Louisiana's Chandeleur Islands (faint arc, lower left) are reshaped by storms. This image illustrates the process, not North Carolina.

credit: NOAA Photo Library / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: An aerial view of damaged buildings and washed-over land on the Bolivar Peninsula after Hurricane Ike.
caption: Bolivar Peninsula, Texas, after Hurricane Ike (2008). Overwash spread sand across the low barrier and destroyed buildings, a process the Outer Banks also experience.

credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: People cross pale limestone blocks separated by deep joints above Malham Cove, England.
caption: Limestone pavement at Malham, Yorkshire Dales, for comparison. Here dissolution has widened joints at the surface; at Mammoth Cave it has enlarged passages deep underground.

credit: Kingsmasher678 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: A karst spring in Alabama flows over rocks from a wooded limestone slope.
caption: A karst spring in Alabama. It shows how water moving through limestone passages re-emerges at the surface, as underground rivers do near Mammoth Cave.

credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · ECOSTRESS, PIA25423 · underlying map attribution retained in image · resized
alt: ECOSTRESS thermal map shows warm urban surfaces in London late at night on 15 July 2022.
caption: ECOSTRESS thermal map of London at night, July 2022. It is not Phoenix, but it shows how measured surface temperatures reveal an urban heat island that an ordinary photograph cannot.

credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · Aqua MODIS / EOSDIS · public domain · resized
alt: Afternoon cumulus clouds over Sri Lanka, observed by Aqua MODIS on 9 April 2013.
caption: Aqua MODIS image of Sri Lanka, April 2013, illustrating the process: cumulus forms over the sun-warmed island as sea-breeze air moves inland, while the cooler sea stays clear.

credit: NOAA GOES-19 / CIMSS, University of Wisconsin–Madison · public domain · 30 October 2025 · resized
alt: GOES-19 satellite view of a cloud-free band beside western Lake Michigan as a land breeze pushes offshore.
caption: GOES-19 satellite image of Lake Michigan, October 2025. A cloud-free band along the shore marks a land breeze, the night-time reverse of a sea breeze.

credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Scientific Visualization Studio · public domain · resized
alt: NASA CERES map of reflected shortwave radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a 0–385 W m⁻² colour scale.
caption: NASA CERES satellite map of reflected sunlight. Snow- and ice-covered regions and cloudy areas reflect strongly; this is reflected energy in W m⁻², not albedo itself.

credit: NASA / Expedition 66 crew · ISS066-E-86970 · public domain · resized
alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
caption: Earth's atmosphere seen edge-on from the ISS. The weather layer is far thicker than Denver's 1.6 km elevation, so the city lies well inside the troposphere.

credit: Paul Wynter / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Graw DFM radiosondes and a radio receiver arranged on a table.
caption: Radiosondes like these are launched twice daily from upper-air stations, including one at Denver. They measure how pressure and temperature change with height.

credit: Syced / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
alt: Dense urban development around Hong Kong's harbour, seen from the hills in 2005.
caption: Hong Kong in 2005. Dense development climbs steep hillsides above the harbour, which is why slope stability matters so much here.

credit: Dexter Perkins / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
alt: Rounded remnants of granite emerge from loose weathered material in an exposed rock profile.
caption: Deeply weathered granite with rounded unweathered cores (location outside Hong Kong). It illustrates saprolite, the weak weathered material that forms many Hong Kong slopes.

credit: Eirian Evans / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: The Thames Barrier's silver piers beside the tidal river in London.
caption: The Thames Barrier in London, for comparison. Like Shanghai's flood walls along the Huangpu, it protects a tidal river city against high water.

credit: Jeff Schmaltz / NASA GSFC · Terra MODIS / LANCE-EOSDIS · public domain · resized
alt: Terra MODIS natural-colour view of Bangladesh, its delta channels and the Sundarbans beside the Bay of Bengal.
caption: Terra MODIS satellite image of the Ganges–Brahmaputra delta, Bangladesh. It shows the process rather than Shanghai: rivers building a low, monsoon-flooded delta plain like the Yangtze delta.

credit: Syced / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
alt: Dense urban development around Hong Kong's harbour, seen from the hills in 2005.
caption: Hong Kong's harbour and high-rise waterfront, which Mangkhut's winds and storm surge struck in September 2018.

credit: AwOiSoAk KaOsIoWa / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: A long bridge over coastal water viewed from Macau Tower.
caption: A bridge over the coastal waters of Macau, in the Pearl River Delta. Mangkhut's storm surge flooded low-lying parts of Macau in 2018.

credit: NASA astronaut Ed Lu / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: The clear eye and tall spiral cloud walls of Hurricane Isabel, photographed from the ISS.
caption: Hurricane Isabel photographed from the ISS in 2003. An Atlantic hurricane and a Pacific typhoon such as Mangkhut are the same kind of storm, with an eye and an eyewall.

credit: Chris Light / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Contour-ploughed fields on the Loess Hills of western Iowa.
caption: Loess Hills, western Iowa, USA. They show the same process as the Loess Plateau: wind-deposited silt that erodes easily once exposed, here farmed along the contours.

credit: US Navy / USDA NRCS Photo Gallery, NRCSIA99138 · public domain · resized
alt: Close-up photograph of a raindrop splashing on soil and throwing droplets and particles outward.
caption: A raindrop striking bare soil (USDA NRCS). Splash detaches particles, the first step in the water erosion that cut the plateau's gullies.
